articles.title: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?
articles.summary: Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workers. On an average workday, Dhruv Amin chats with dozens of colleagues to get things done at his AI startup Anything.
body: But none of these co-workers are people. They’re artificial intelligence agents, software that handles tasks without human intervention. Anything is one of several startups building them, and betting on a future where workplaces will increasingly turn over their sales, marketing, coding and other tasks to semi-autonomous AI. At Anything, there are 15 human employees and roughly 150 agents – a ratio that Amin believes will soon be the norm.
“I think in a year, every company will have more AI co-workers than human co-workers,” he said.

In the San Francisco tech scene, agents have quickly become a new status symbol, showing that a company can do more with less, several startup employees said. It’s common for workers to brag about how well their agents can handle common office drudgery like answering emails or help with essential business operations such as giving sales pitches.

But agents are also creating tension. They are alienating customers and colleagues who seek human interaction, eliminating roles and forcing employees to become overnight managers of the bots that often make mistakes.

articles.title: ‘Algorithms make everything predictable’: why the CD is making a comeback
articles.summary: As John Lewis reports a 96% rise in searches for CD players, music fans share their reasons for ditching streaming. CDs appear to be having a resurgence. John Lewis said searches for CD players are up 96% since July, while another report on trends in music and film this year found that CD sales are…
body: With this in mind, we asked music fans why they favour discs over other formats, and if it is a new preference or a lifetime habit.

Andrew Wales, 67, from London, owns “well over 10,000” CDs. “My wife’s very considerate,” he says over the phone. “There’s quite a few in this room where I’m speaking.” They have also spilt into the next bedroom and into the corridor.

“I don’t need Spotify,” says Wales. “The fact is, I like listening to music and I have always preferred owning it in a physical form. The [size of the] CD format allows me to own the number I own despite living in a two-bedroom flat and not a country mansion, so that’s another bonus.”

Much of the classical music Wales buys and listens to is available only on CD. “I bought my first CD in 1991 – John Scofield, Meant to Be – around the same time that I bought my first CD player. LPs were becoming increasingly shoddy, both in terms of pressing and presentation, and their limitations meant that often or not songs or tracks were included on the CD release, but not on LP. There are still cases where that happens today.”

articles.title: Tiny basement turned ‘exuberant’ apartment wins interior prize at Australia’s National Architecture awards
articles.summary: With a footprint of less than 40 sq metres, the Melbourne project required careful planning – and some spatial trickery. Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email. Last week on a balmy spring evening, Ronnen Goren and his partner had dinner in a small pavilion on their terrace for the first time.
body: This domestic scene took place in a semi-subterranean former laundry in inner Melbourne – a space of less than 40 sq metres that was renovated at the end of 2024. On 29 October, the “exuberant” reimagining of the damp basement space in Toorak, on the grounds of the heritage-listed Quamby apartment complex, received the Emil Sodersten award for interior architecture at Australia’s National Architecture awards.

Originally designed as a service space by the acclaimed Australian architect Roy Grounds in 1941, its recent rebirth was overseen by Timothy Hill of Partners Hill. The project, titled Studio8, has transformed a poorly executed 1970s apartment conversion into an ambient retreat that belies its tiny footprint.

In 2022, despite the apartment’s “grim” condition, Goren says he and his partner were drawn to its “amazing location” and its “heritage and provenance”, not to mention the north-facing courtyard that’s almost bigger than the apartment. They lived in it as it was for about 18 months, “just imagining what it could be”.
That’s where Hill – whose interest in converting secondary spaces into quality housing stock dates back to his university days – came in.

articles.title: Behind the scenes at the scream park: fear, fainting, clowns – and ‘code brown’
articles.summary: At Norfolk’s ‘premier scare attraction’ there are ghouls, chainsaws, satanic cults and a haunted hospital. But what goes on behind the scenes? ‘We always say to the scare actors, you’re going to think the boys will be the worst.
body: This is part of the workplace induction at PrimEvil, one of many immersive “scream parks” that pop up across the UK in the lead up to Halloween. For about £40 a ticket, groups of all ages spend the night roaming themed attractions and being terrorised by actors and special effects. Though the risks are minimal, the spikes in heart rate are very real.

For Francis and the rest of the team, PrimEvil is months in the making. The nightly production involves more than 100 actors and dozens of crew, spread across six themed attractions, each drawing from familiar horror tropes – the scary clowns at the Circus of Terror, the cannibalistic trailer-dwellers over at Route 666, the satanic cult of The Offering. The winding routes are designed to disorient you with strobe lights, smoke machines, mirrored walls, hidden doors, false exits and unstable floors. But it’s down to the performers to bring the nightmare to life.

articles.title: How the Best Peptide Skin-Care Can Deliver Botox-Like Results
articles.summary: Peptides skincare—a.k.a. the “silent powerhouse”—can do everything from stimulate collagen and elastin production to slow down to cellular processes.
body: Given all the peptides buzz, you might be wondering what the best peptide skin-care products can do for you, and if they really are the gold standard of anti-aging skincare. These “silent powerhouses” (there are, in fact, various types of peptides) are a derm favorite for healing skin, slowing aging, and stimulating collagen, reducing puffiness, and boosting skin elasticity. At their most basic, peptides are short chains of amino acids that form the building blocks of proteins like collagen, elastin, and keratin. These proteins are essential for firm, youthful-looking skin.

According to board-certified dermatologist Brendan Camp, MD, peptides are garnering a lot of attention right now because they offer a range of skin benefits without being harsh or irritating. Unlike some ingredients that have had their moment in the spotlight and since faded from focus, peptides for skin tend to be well-tolerated and easy to incorporate into a daily routine, which is why they are likely here to stay. He also notes that peptides can be especially helpful during post-procedure recovery, since they support the skin barrier and aid overall healing.
points: Peptides skincare—a.k.a. the “silent powerhouse”—can do everything from stimulate collagen and elastin production to slow down to cellular processes.

If you want reliable earbuds that cost less than tonight's dinner, JBL is a reliable brand to fall back on, with plenty of budget-friendly models that lack the bells and…
body: These earbuds aren’t reinventing the wheel, but they do check important boxes. They last up to eight hours without the charging case, and up to 32 hours with the case. Ten minutes of charging will get you a couple of hours of playback, and they have an IP54 rating, making them dust- and splash-resistant. The built-in mics work well in reasonably quiet rooms, but may struggle to separate your voice from loud background noise. Another perk is Find My Buds, which helps locate misplaced earbuds via a sound that’s played.

With 8 mm dynamic drivers, they deliver punchy bass that translates well to adrenaline-pumping workout music, and adequate vocal clarity for music and podcasts. Though the default tuning is relatively balanced, you can tweak it on the app’s equalizer to adjust it to your liking. They lack ANC and Bluetooth multipoint pairing, which isn’t surprising given the price point, but still pack in a solid amount of features and quality into $30, making the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds a good value for everyday bargain earbuds that get the job done.

articles.title: It’s Time for Witchcore Interiors
articles.summary: The season of the witch has arrived—and whether it’s a few more candles, a Gothic bed, or folkloric textiles, you too can have a home that’s a little more bewitching.
body: Being a witch is not just for Halloween. There is a genuine resurgence of witchcraft afoot, especially among Gen Z, who are embracing ritualistic magic as a lifestyle—and one with far more positive associations than the historically stigmatized archetype.

Perhaps in a world that feels like it’s falling apart at the seams—and for those not part of an organized religion, who now make up roughly a quarter of the global population, according to Pew—it is tempting to seek sanctuary in magical forces. Plus, in the age of social media and AI agents plugged into every aspect of your life, there’s something alluring about a bit of mystery; the glow of candles over screen time.

There’s a deeper urge driving the witchcraft revival too: reclaiming power in a world that continues to diminish women—their voices, bodies, and rights. As the founders of the new feminist publication Witch Magazine say, “witch” is a term “historically weaponized to silence and oppress those who challenge the status quo.”

articles.title: This Intimate Wedding on Lake Como Felt Like “A Garden Party in the Clouds”
articles.summary: For their three-day celebration at Villa Balbiano, Alyssa Choo and Erik Lowe brought a little of New York to Italy—with 54 close family and friends, a custom Vera Wang gown, and a fireworks-filled finale.
body: In November 2020, in the middle of the pandemic, Alyssa Choo downloaded Tinder and matched with Erik Lowe that same day. “I was living downtown after graduating from Barnard College, while Erik had just returned to New York City from San Francisco after his CEO gave him the opportunity to work remotely,” Alyssa recalls.

As luck would have it, Erik had just moved into an apartment five blocks from Alyssa’s. That same week, they met for brunch at Ruby’s in Nolita. “It was pleasant enough, but nothing that suggested a love story was underway,” Alyssa remembers. “I went quiet on him for two weeks afterward.”

Then one day, while scrolling through Instagram, Alyssa came across a post of Erik and two friends sitting on a Central Park bench. The caption simply read “six feet”—a nod to the social-distancing rules of the time. It made her laugh, and minutes later, she finally responded to his last message. Their second date was dinner at Bond Street, where they had the entire restaurant to themselves—one of the stranger perks of dating during a pandemic. From then on, they were inseparable.
